plan.title: Phishing by numbers
plan.businessGoal: At Quillon Freight (fictional company), raise the share of employees who report a phishing drill to the security desk from 1 in 7 to 1 in 2 by the end of 2026, and keep password entries in drills under 2%.

audience.role: Every employee of Quillon Freight (fictional), a freight and logistics company of 1,200 people: office staff, drivers and warehouse teams who read email at work
audience.notes: Have all received the monthly drills since January 2025. Know the Report button exists; most do not know what happens after they press it, nor which lures work best on them.

sources.title: Quillon Freight security desk, phishing and incident report 2025 (internal report, fictional)
Quillon Freight phishing drills, results from January to November 2025 (internal report, fictional)
Quillon Freight information security policy and the history of its rules (internal policy, fictional)

objectives.statement: Spot the signs of phishing in a work email: an unexpected request for a password, money or a file, and a sender or link that does not match who it claims to be.
objectives.criterion: Right choice in a realistic email scenario, with the signs named in the feedback

objectives.statement: Report a suspicious email with the Report button rather than replying or forwarding it, and call the security desk at once after a click or a typed password.
objectives.criterion: Chooses to report in the scenario; names the call to 4444 after a click

items.title: Phishing at Quillon, in three numbers
items.description: Three figures frame the module: 1,840 phishing emails reported in 2025, 62% of security incidents started by an email, and a phish now blocked 11 minutes after the first report (4 h 10 in 2022).

items.title: Where attacks start and what they look like
items.description: Where the 74 incidents of 2025 started (email far ahead of websites, phone calls and USB sticks), and what the 1,840 phishing emails pretended to be: delivery notices, invoices, password resets, payroll messages.

items.title: How a phish catches people
items.description: The January 2025 drill as a funnel (1,200 sent, 790 opened, 384 clicked, 100 typed a password) and the 1 in 7 who reported it; then the lures placed by how often they come and how often people click: invoices and password resets are frequent and convincing.

items.title: What reporting and drills changed
items.description: The learner predicts the click rate of the November drill (5%, from 32% in January), then sees that every team clicks less and the warehouse still most; reports per month before and after the one-click Report button (2023); each rule of the policy answered an attack (two-step sign-in, Report button, supplier call-back, drills).

items.title: What to do with a suspicious email
items.description: Pause, check, report, and call 4444 after a click, with an unscored check question on what to do first after a click; what a report sets off (triage, block for all 1,200 inboxes, warning, next drill); the decision path for an unexpected email.

items.title: Your turn: new bank details
items.description: Unscored decision: an email from a known supplier's lookalike address asks Finance to pay this week's invoice to new bank details. Report it, reply to check, or forward it to Finance, with feedback on each.

spacing: Monthly: a drill, debrief for those who click
D+30: each team's drill figures, by its manager

validation.reference: elabora-core sample course, not a real client approval
